title: Rethinking State Tracking in Recurrent Models Through Error Control Dynamics
claim: Models with state-independent dynamics cannot contract injected errors, while state-dependent models actively and selectively correct them.
layout: 6 columns grouped Affine vs State-dependent; 3D trajectories above, log-error curves below
description: Two rows by six columns of small plots, one column per model. A bold gray header groups the first four columns as Affine (Mamba, Mamba-3, Negative Mamba, Token-gated RNN) and the last two as State-dependent (tanh RNN, State-gated RNN). A vertical dashed line separates the groups. The top row shows 3D trajectory plots with axes PC1, PC2 and steps (0 to 179). Crosses mark scattered injected errors and a green dashed line marks zero error. Red (Mamba, Mamba-3), gold (Negative Mamba, Token-gated) and blue (tanh, State-gated) lines converge or diverge. The Token-gated RNN trajectories fan out into a large yellow cloud. The bottom row shows log-scale error ratio versus steps after injection. The affine curves are flat, slowly decaying or rising, while the blue curves drop sharply by several orders of magnitude. The eye goes first to the yellow explosion and the blue collapse.
caption: Perturbation recovery after noise injection on $S_3$. Top: error trajectories in a fixed 2D PCA basis of the injected errors; $\times$ marks the injected error, $\circ$ the endpoint (filled when clipped off scale), and the green dashed line and $+$ zero error. Bottom: normalized error magnitude $\|e_t\|/\|e_{t_0}\|$ over time, median and interquartile range over trials; thin lines show individual trials, and the dashed line a ratio of $1$. Affine models show either global decay (Mamba, Mamba-3, and Negative Mamba) or expansion (Token-gated RNN), while state-dependent models (tanh RNN and State-gated RNN) show strong, selective error contraction.
abstract: The theory of state tracking in recurrent architectures has predominantly focused on expressive capacity: whether a fixed architecture can theoretically realize a set of symbolic transition rules. We argue that equally important is error control, the dynamics governing hidden-state drift along the directions that distinguish symbolic states. We prove that affine recurrent networks, a class of models encompassing State-Space Models and Linear Attention, cannot correct errors along state-separating subspaces once they preserve state representations. Consequently, practical affine trackers do not learn robust state tracking; rather, they learn finite-horizon solutions governed by accumulated state-relevant error. We characterize the mechanics of this failure, showing that tracking remains readable only while the accumulating within-class spread remains small relative to the between-class separation. We demonstrate empirically on group state-tracking tasks that this breakdown is predictable: tracking collapses when the distinguishability ratio crosses the readability threshold. Across trained models, the point of this crossing predicts the horizon at which downstream accuracy fails. These results establish that robust state tracking is determined not only by an architecture's theoretical expressivity but crucially by its error control.
